appraisal_events.evidence: To Mme Verdurin's proposal to invite «Madame de Molé» the baron opposes an absolute veto and a tirade — «une pécore sans naissance, sans loyauté, sans esprit», «cette petite grenouille bourgeoise», «Voilà un nom qu'il ne faut plus prononcer, ou bien je n'ai qu'à me retirer» — after having struck out every other name she proposed; the narration notes that no one, the countess included, ever discovered what she had done, and that his exclusions rest on «des ressentiments de toqué» or «des habiletés d'acteur».
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Molé is barred from a party held in her hostess's own house and abused at length; the narration ironizes the verdict by exposing the arbitrary machinery of Charlus's favour and disfavour rather than endorsing his grounds.

appraisal_events.evidence: After his lecture on «eugénique sociale» — «On est ainsi soi-même, quand on sait m'écouter, l'accoucheur de son destin» — the narration cuts in: «Il était trop évident que M. de Charlus n'avait pas su agir sur le sien ; agir est autre chose que parler, même avec éloquence.» His genealogical verdicts are shown to reverse themselves according to his quarrels, his exclusions to be an actor's way of refilling the house for an unchanged number, and he offends his hostess «sans se rendre compte»; the evening ends with his furtive cruising talk likened to lunatics whispering «C'est Jeanne d'Arc», while he parades with Morel «à étaler ainsi publiquement leur intimité secrète».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration systematically undercuts the baron's eloquence and authority, presenting his social power as compulsive, self-deceived and, in this house, already the object of a plot against him.

appraisal_events.evidence: «La force de Mme Verdurin, c'était l'amour sincère qu'elle avait de l'art, la peine qu'elle se donnait pour les fidèles, les merveilleux dîners... Chez Mme Verdurin la troupe était parfaite, entraînée, le répertoire de premier ordre, il ne manquait que le public»; having patiently gathered the unusable scraps of what would one day be her salon, she is now seen «toujours... dans une première loge... à côté de la princesse Yourbeletief», «au premier rang» of the Russian-ballet enthusiasm, her suppers gathering Stravinski and Strauss with «les plus grandes dames de Paris et les Altesses étrangères».
appraisal_events.explanation: A sustained narratorial account credits her with real artistic sincerity and traces her rise to the first rank of Paris, witnessed by the whole fashionable world, even as it calls her a «vieille fée Carabosse, mais toute-puissante».

appraisal_events.evidence: Told of her dying friend, she answers before the faithful «de tristesse je n'en éprouve aucune... ça ne m'a presque rien fait», refuses to postpone the party, and, seconded by M. Verdurin («je t'ai toujours dit qu'elle avait mauvaise réputation»), declares that reputation «universellement connu ; pas mauvaise, mais honteuse, déshonorante»; the faithful listen «avec le mélange d'admiration et de malaise» proper to a cruelly realistic play.
appraisal_events.explanation: The dead woman is publicly denied both mourning and honour in the salon where she was a faithful; the narration ironizes the hostess's proclaimed sincerity by anatomizing the vanity and convenience behind it.

status_effects.explanation: A boundary is closed against her: struck from the guest list of the quai Conti party and from the baron's familiarity, on pain of his own withdrawal.
She must swallow the baron's vetoes in her own house — «déçue et furieuse», feeling «atteinte son autorité de Patronne» — because she still needs the guests only he can bring.
The narration's verdict is severe: eloquent but incapable of acting on his own destiny, arbitrary in his judgments, theatrical in his exclusions, and blind to the hostility he is provoking.

He is discredited by association: the passage opens on «le rôle ridicule et odieux que lui faisait jouer M. de Charlus» and shows the baron publicly displaying their intimacy and planning to adopt him.

Distinct from tonight's setback: her standing in the world is shown to have risen to the first rank, publicly registered in the front box at the Opéra and at suppers the greatest ladies and foreign Highnesses attend.
Her standing collapses before witnesses: her death is declared to cost her closest hostess nothing, her party is not postponed, and her reputation is pronounced shameful and dishonouring.
The narration exposes her proclaimed frankness as hardness dressed up as originality, and the faithful's admiration is mixed with unease at what her house would make of their own deaths.

ambiguities: The dying and then dead «princesse», Mme Verdurin's «grande amie», is never named in the passage; she matches the princesse Sherbatoff of the reference sheet as a faithful of the little clan, but no surface form in the passage establishes that, so she is kept unresolved.
